title: The whole text: structure, perspective, rhetoric, tone and pragmatics

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Analyse paragraph- and text-level structure, narrative perspective, rhetorical devices, and tone, register and pragmatics.

blocks.heading: Structure and cohesion
blocks.text: Structure is how a whole text is organised: its opening, sequence, shifts of focus, paragraphing and ending. Sentence structure is a feature of language; "structure" alone means the whole text. Cohesion is the ties that link sentences and paragraphs — discourse markers, reference and repetition. A discourse marker signals a step in the talk (however, meanwhile, first) rather than contributing content. Anaphoric reference points back to something already mentioned; cataphoric reference points forward, creating an expectation the reader carries until it is met.

blocks.heading: What to track in a whole text
blocks.text: The structural features worth tracking are the opening, shifts of focus, paragraph length, sequence, repetition across the text, and the ending. Two moves repay attention. A one-sentence paragraph stands out against the paragraphs around it, so a writer can use one to mark a turning point: after three long paragraphs of account, "That was the last time we trusted the gauge." lands as a door closing. A cyclical structure returns to its opening image or idea at the end, which makes the ending feel like an arrival and frames what changed in between: the same river at the start and the close, in a different light.

blocks.heading: Location is not structure analysis
blocks.text: Leaving structure out, or saying where things are without saying what the arrangement does, is the commonest structural error. A structural point names the arrangement (an opening, a shift, a return) and its effect on the reader: "the account of the rescue is held back until the final paragraph, so the reader spends the piece asking whether it succeeded, which is how the piece creates suspense." That sentence could not be written by someone who only knows where the paragraph is.

blocks.heading: Narrative perspective
blocks.text: First-person narration is told by an "I" inside the story; it gives closeness and limits what the reader knows to what that narrator knows, so the reader can be surprised with the narrator, or misled by them. Second-person address puts the reader inside the text as "you", involving them directly. Third-person narration is limited when it stays with one character’s knowledge, omniscient when it moves freely and reports what no single character could know. The narrator is the voice inside the text; the author is the person who wrote it — a first-person narrator who is wrong about something is not the author being wrong.

blocks.heading: Rhetorical devices
blocks.text: A rhetorical question expects no answer, because the answer is assumed; it works by making the audience supply the answer the writer wants, so the analysis names the answer it invites. Direct address uses you or your to put the reader in the sentence. A tricolon is a list of three with a rhythm that builds to a close; anaphora repeats a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses; antithesis sets opposed ideas in balance; hyperbole exaggerates for effect.

blocks.heading: Worked example: a question and its answer
blocks.text: A writer asks: "Do we want a town where the last cinema is a parking lot?" The question expects no answer; the answer it invites is "no", and the reader supplies it, which is the mechanism: having said "no" in their own head, the reader has joined the writer’s side before the argument begins. The analysis names that invited answer, or it has said nothing the label "rhetorical question" did not already say.

blocks.heading: Questions and loose terms
blocks.text: Two errors recur. A question is rhetorical only when the text does not answer it and no real answer is being waited for; a question that the text goes on to answer, or that genuinely seeks information, is not rhetorical. And a narrative term is used only when the example has the feature the term names: stream of consciousness is a continuous unpunctuated flow of a mind, not any first-person account, and a loose term undermines the analysis, because the point built on it falls with the label.

blocks.heading: Tone, register and pragmatics
blocks.text: Tone is the attitude a text conveys towards its subject or reader, and it is a result of choices, so the analysis names the choices that create it. Register is the variety of language suited to a situation, marked chiefly by formality and vocabulary; a formal register is right or wrong only for an audience and a purpose — a formal blog is as mismatched as a casual report to officials. Formality is marked by contractions, slang, first person and spoken markers on the informal side, and by nominalisation and Latinate vocabulary on the formal side. Pragmatics is meaning that comes from context and implication rather than the words alone; implicature is what a writer implies without stating it.

blocks.heading: Three separate questions
blocks.text: How common a word is, how formal it is, and the tone of the text are three separate questions. An everyday word can sit in a formal text ("the committee met"), and a rare word can be slang. Ask them separately: is the word everyday or rare? is it formal or informal? what attitude do the choices add up to? A shift of register inside a text signals a change in the writer’s relationship with the reader: a report that ends "and honestly, we were tired" has admitted the reader to confidence, and the drop is the point.

blocks.heading: Worked example: one paragraph, all three levels
blocks.text: Take a two-sentence opening from a feature on a drought year: "The river we swam in as boys is now a line of cracked mud. You can walk where the water was, and the fish you used to chase lie in the shade of the bridge that no longer crosses anything." The language level is personified absence — the river that "no longer crosses anything" makes the bridge the failure, and the second person "you can walk" puts the reader inside the dry bed. The structure level is an opening that plants an image and a promise: the piece will be about what the loss did to the town, and the reader has been handed the before ("as boys") and the after in two sentences. The whole-text level, which the analysis reaches for next, is the question of what the piece does with this opening — whether it returns to the image, whether it blames, whether it ends in the mud or the memory. One extract, three levels: an analysis that keeps them distinct is already organised.

blocks.heading: Where this vocabulary is used
blocks.text: Every later topic leans on these terms: the directed response in topic 1.4 is judged by the features a form carries, and the comparison beside it lives on the differences between two texts’ registers and sentence structures; the commentary in topic 2.1 asks for exactly the feature, evidence, effect moves taught here; the argumentative writing of topic 2.4 deploys the rhetorical devices as choices to make rather than to analyse. Learn the terms as tools now, and the tasks become places to use them.

blocks.heading: In the exam
blocks.text: This topic is the vocabulary of the analysis questions on Paper 1 and the reflective commentary on Paper 2: forty of the hundred AS marks are for analysis, and every analysis rests on exact terms. The names here are a working set, not a closed list: the syllabus offers its linguistic elements as suggestions of what to know, and a feature the notes have not named can still be analysed well if the analysis names the choice, quotes the words, states the effect on this reader, and links the effect to the text’s purpose.
